summary: Mars Analog Finder takes any Mars coordinate and searches the whole land surface of Earth for terrain that resembles it. Mars and Earth elevation data are cut into identical 32 km patches at 500 m per pixel. Each patch is turned into a shape descriptor (slope, curvature, roughness at several scales, spectral shape), and the Mars patch is compared in all 8 orientations against an index of Earth patches. The shortlisted matches are then re-ranked with physical checks drawn from NASA Earth observations: rainfall, vegetation, albedo, surface-temperature range and a thermal-inertia proxy. Each result comes with a side-by-side image and a table showing where the analogy holds and where it breaks, including factors Earth can’t reproduce, such as gravity, air pressure and radiation. It targets analogs beyond the well-known Atacama and Antarctic sites.
details:
What it does:

Mars Analog Finder takes any Mars coordinate and searches Earth for terrain that resembles it. It returns ranked Earth locations, a side-by-side hillshade comparison, and a per-factor table showing where the analogy holds and where it breaks.

How it works:

  1. Earth elevation (NASADEM) and Mars elevation (MOLA + HRSC blend) are cut into identical 32 km patches at 500 m per pixel, so both planets are compared at the same scale.
  2. Each patch becomes a 38-number terrain-shape descriptor (slope distribution, curvature, multi-scale roughness, spectral shape, relief). The Mars patch is tried in all 8 rotations and flips. FAISS finds the nearest Earth patches by Euclidean distance, and the similarity is calibrated against the distance to the whole index, so a weak shortlist can’t show a perfect score.
  3. The shortlist is filtered (dense vegetation, heavy rainfall, sea and lake patches are removed) and re-scored with physical gates: albedo (Mars TES vs MODIS), aridity (GPM IMERG), vegetation (MODIS NDVI), slope, roughness, relief, surface pressure and latitude. Thermal inertia, temperature, ice and mineral gates are built into the code and switch on when a matching Mars raster is supplied.
  4. Every search prints a gate report listing which gates ran, which were skipped and why, and which used an assumed value. A gate never guesses a Mars value silently.
  5. Four ranking profiles (balanced, mobility, ice, minerals) re-weight the same index for different exploration goals. Known unscorable mismatches (gravity, atmosphere, radiation, liquid-water alteration) are listed with every result.

Results:

In a test search for Jezero crater (18.4°N, 77.5°E), restricted to the Atacama DEM box, the top matches were near (-23.7, -68.5), (-26.6, -67.5) and (-20.9, -69.4), with final scores around 0.60 to 0.63 Terrain shape matched strongly, while aridity and vegetation matched, and albedo matched partially (Earth ~0.19–0.23 vs Mars 0.13). The pressure gate shows a mismatch, as expected, since Earth’s air is always far thicker.

Why it matters:

Analog sites are usually chosen by reputation. This gives a repeatable, data-driven way to search for them, and shows which properties an analog shares with Mars and which it doesn’t, so mission teams know what a field test on that site can and can’t teach them.

Limitations:

The Earth index covers only the Atacama region downloaded for this submission, so results show the best match within that region, not on all of Earth. Mars thermal inertia, temperature, hydrogen and mineral rasters were not loaded, so those gates are inactive. The pipeline was tested on synthetic data and run on real NASA data only for this region.

Tools:

Python, NumPy, SciPy, pandas, rasterio, h5py, pyhdf, FAISS, matplotlib, earthaccess, Kaggle Notebooks.

Creativity:

It uses retrieval, like an image search, over terrain shape first, then physical checks. It’s goal-switchable, and it explains mismatches instead of hiding them.

Use of AI. Code and text were developed with Claude (Anthropic), then run, tested and debugged by the team.
